current_density.note: current_normalization 'geometric_area' is inferred from the 1 cm2 GDE (page 10-11, Methods, Electrode preparation); the source gives mA cm-2 but does not state the normalization basis explicitly.

electrode_potential.note: Potential under each held current not printed in the main text (chronopotentiometry profiles are in the SI, which is not appended)

evidence.quote: Each catalyst was subsequently tested under a series of constant current densities of 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 mA cm⁻2, with each electrolysis step conducted for 1 h (Figure S11-S17)

and the gaseous products were quantified using online gas chromatography (GC) equipped with a thermal conductor detector (TCD), while the liquid products were quantified using proton nuclear magnetic resonance (¹H NMR).

Typically, the electron mole fraction required for each product formation was used along with the product mole fraction and total charge consumed for each period to calculate the Faradaic efficiency (FEs).
The resulting FE profiles for all catalysts are summarized in Figure 5a–c, which present FE(H2), FE(CO), and FE(HCOOH) as a function of current density
in our case, incorporation of MoS2 into Ti-based MXenes did not yield a notable improvement in CO2RR selectivity.
As shown in Figure 5a-c, both composites continue to exhibit high FE(H₂) values (>70 % across current densities) with only marginal increases in FE(CO) relative to the pristine MXenes (Figure 5b).
FE(HCOOH) remained below 15 % in all cases (Figure 5c).

evidence.quote: Each catalyst was subsequently tested under a series of constant current densities of 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 mA cm⁻2, with each electrolysis step conducted for 1 h (Figure S11-S17)

and the gaseous products were quantified using online gas chromatography (GC) equipped with a thermal conductor detector (TCD), while the liquid products were quantified using proton nuclear magnetic resonance (¹H NMR).

Typically, the electron mole fraction required for each product formation was used along with the product mole fraction and total charge consumed for each period to calculate the Faradaic efficiency (FEs).
The resulting FE profiles for all catalysts are summarized in Figure 5a–c, which present FE(H2), FE(CO), and FE(HCOOH) as a function of current density
A similar pattern was observed for the Ti4N3Tx which exhibits a slightly higher initial FE(H₂) (~82 %) and comparable FE(CO) behavior.
CO production remains modest, with the maximum FE(CO) of ~20% recorded at 30 mA cm⁻2.

in FE(CO) with current density may suggest that at moderate overpotentials, a fraction of surface sites begin to stabilize COOH intermediates, but the effect is not sufficient to overcome the competing HER pathway.

props.name: V2CTx MXene CO2 reduction at 10 mA cm-2 (1 h)

current_density.note: current_normalization 'geometric_area' is inferred from the 1 cm2 GDE (page 10-11, Methods, Electrode preparation); the source gives mA cm-2 but does not state the normalization basis explicitly.

electrode_potential.note: Potential under each held current not printed in the main text (chronopotentiometry profiles are in the SI, which is not appended)

evidence.quote: Each catalyst was subsequently tested under a series of constant current densities of 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 mA cm⁻2, with each electrolysis step conducted for 1 h (Figure S11-S17)

and the gaseous products were quantified using online gas chromatography (GC) equipped with a thermal conductor detector (TCD), while the liquid products were quantified using proton nuclear magnetic resonance (¹H NMR).

Typically, the electron mole fraction required for each product formation was used along with the product mole fraction and total charge consumed for each period to calculate the Faradaic efficiency (FEs).
The resulting FE profiles for all catalysts are summarized in Figure 5a–c, which present FE(H2), FE(CO), and FE(HCOOH) as a function of current density
the vanadium-based MXenes significantly enhanced CO2 reduction selectivity.

Both V2NTx and V2CTx exhibited markedly lower FE(H₂) compared with Titanium-based MXenes, while FE(CO) and FE(HCOOH) increased substantially, reaching ~35–50% and 15–20%, respectively, at current densities of 25–30 mA cm⁻2.
Notably, only CO and HCOOH were detected as CO2 reduction products, corresponding to gas- and liquid-phase, respectively.
At higher current densities (>40 mA cm⁻2), HER activity again becomes prominent, as evidenced by the rise in FE(H2).
Moreover, the concurrent generation of CO and H2 at tunable ratios gives rise to a controllable CO/H2 (syngas) mixture

A more substantial enhancement arose from changing the metal center: V-based MXenes shifted the reaction pathway toward CO2RR, with V2NTx achieving FE(CO) ~50% and FE(HCOOH) ~18%, outperforming V2CTx and suppressing HER at moderate current densities.
V is more beneficial than with C. For instance, V2NTx achieved FE of approximately 50% for CO and 18% for HCOOH, while V2CTx yielded 35% for CO and 15% for HCOOH under the same conditions.

electrode_potential.as_reported: the applied potential for V2NTx gradually shifted from approximately –1.25 V to –1.156 V vs RHE, while that of V2CTx shifted from approximately –1.22 V to –1.17 V vs RHE
electrode_potential.note: Initial value on the RHE scale; the potential drifts during electrolysis.

evidence.quote: Both electrodes were tested at a fixed current density of 30 mA cm-2, corresponding to the potential range in which the highest FE(CO) values were previously observed.
Continuous electrolysis was carried out for ~22 hours in a CO2-purged 1 M KHCO3 electrolyte using the same flow-cell configuration employed in earlier measurements.
During electrolysis, the applied potential for V2NTx gradually shifted from approximately –1.25 V to –1.156 V vs RHE, while that of V2CTx shifted from approximately –1.22 V to –1.17 V vs RHE.
Despite these slight positive drifts, both catalysts maintained nearly constant FE(CO) values of ≈ 50 % (V2NTx) and ≈ 35 % (V2CTx) throughout the ~22 hours duration.
The stable FE(CO) under continuous electrolysis demonstrates that the CO-producing sites remain catalytically active over extended operation without significant deactivation or selectivity loss.
Long-term stability measurements of (a) V2NTx and (b) V2CTx MXene catalysts for CO2 reduction to CO in CO2-purged 1 M KHCO3 electrolyte at a constant current density
we found that the V-based catalysts were stable over hours of reaction time with no loss in FE for CO.
V-based materials also displayed stability over hours with no loss in CO selectivity.

current_density.note: current_normalization 'geometric_area' is inferred from the 1 cm2 GDE (page 10-11, Methods, Electrode preparation); the source gives mA cm-2 but does not state the normalization basis explicitly.

evidence.quote: Each catalyst was subsequently tested under a series of constant current densities of 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 mA cm⁻2, with each electrolysis step conducted for 1 h (Figure S11-S17)

and the gaseous products were quantified using online gas chromatography (GC) equipped with a thermal conductor detector (TCD), while the liquid products were quantified using proton nuclear magnetic resonance (¹H NMR).

Typically, the electron mole fraction required for each product formation was used along with the product mole fraction and total charge consumed for each period to calculate the Faradaic efficiency (FEs).
The resulting FE profiles for all catalysts are summarized in Figure 5a–c, which present FE(H2), FE(CO), and FE(HCOOH) as a function of current density
the vanadium-based MXenes significantly enhanced CO2 reduction selectivity.

Both V2NTx and V2CTx exhibited markedly lower FE(H₂) compared with Titanium-based MXenes, while FE(CO) and FE(HCOOH) increased substantially, reaching ~35–50% and 15–20%, respectively, at current densities of 25–30 mA cm⁻2.
Notably, only CO and HCOOH were detected as CO2 reduction products, corresponding to gas- and liquid-phase, respectively.
At higher current densities (>40 mA cm⁻2), HER activity again becomes prominent, as evidenced by the rise in FE(H2).
Moreover, the concurrent generation of CO and H2 at tunable ratios gives rise to a controllable CO/H2 (syngas) mixture

A more substantial enhancement arose from changing the metal center: V-based MXenes shifted the reaction pathway toward CO2RR, with V2NTx achieving FE(CO) ~50% and FE(HCOOH) ~18%, outperforming V2CTx and suppressing HER at moderate current densities.
V is more beneficial than with C. For instance, V2NTx achieved FE of approximately 50% for CO and 18% for HCOOH, while V2CTx yielded 35% for CO and 15% for HCOOH under the same conditions.

props.name: V2NTx MXene long-term CO2 reduction stability at 30 mA cm-2 (~22 h)

current_density.note: current_normalization 'geometric_area' is inferred from the 1 cm2 GDE (page 10-11, Methods, Electrode preparation); the source gives mA cm-2 but does not state the normalization basis explicitly.

electrode_potential.as_reported: the applied potential for V2NTx gradually shifted from approximately –1.25 V to –1.156 V vs RHE, while that of V2CTx shifted from approximately –1.22 V to –1.17 V vs RHE
electrode_potential.note: Initial value on the RHE scale; the potential drifts during electrolysis.

evidence.quote: Both electrodes were tested at a fixed current density of 30 mA cm-2, corresponding to the potential range in which the highest FE(CO) values were previously observed.
Continuous electrolysis was carried out for ~22 hours in a CO2-purged 1 M KHCO3 electrolyte using the same flow-cell configuration employed in earlier measurements.
During electrolysis, the applied potential for V2NTx gradually shifted from approximately –1.25 V to –1.156 V vs RHE, while that of V2CTx shifted from approximately –1.22 V to –1.17 V vs RHE.
Despite these slight positive drifts, both catalysts maintained nearly constant FE(CO) values of ≈ 50 % (V2NTx) and ≈ 35 % (V2CTx) throughout the ~22 hours duration.
The stable FE(CO) under continuous electrolysis demonstrates that the CO-producing sites remain catalytically active over extended operation without significant deactivation or selectivity loss.
Long-term stability measurements of (a) V2NTx and (b) V2CTx MXene catalysts for CO2 reduction to CO in CO2-purged 1 M KHCO3 electrolyte at a constant current density
we found that the V-based catalysts were stable over hours of reaction time with no loss in FE for CO.
V-based materials also displayed stability over hours with no loss in CO selectivity.
